study.title: Ezekiel 10 The gradual withdrawal of the glory of the Lord and the proclamation of judgment
study.overview: The chapter resumes the same glorious vision already seen by Ezekiel in the river Chebar and applies it to Jerusalem. In the temple, the presence of God appears above the cherubim, the man clothed in linen receives coals to spread them over the city, and the glory of the Lord goes away in stages: from the cherub to the entrance of the house, then into the courtyard, and finally to the east gate. The vision unites holiness, judgment and abandonment: the divine presence is not treated as the property of the temple, but as holy glory that departs before the uncleanness of the people.

outline.title: The glory in the temple and the embers of judgment
outline.explanation: Ezekiel seeth the throne upon the cherubim, and the man clothed with linen receives embers to throw them upon the city. The cloud fills the temple and the courtyard, showing both the majesty of God and the beginning of the imminent judgment upon Jerusalem.

outline.title: The fire between the cherubim and the presence that moves
outline.explanation: The sound of the wings, the human hand under the wings and the fire taken from among the cherubim reinforce the solemn reality of vision. The action is carefully conducted by the divine order, showing that judgment is not accidental, but directed by the Lord.

outline.title: The wheels, faces and the providential government
outline.explanation: The wheels with the cherubim, full of eyes, and the four faces point to the mobility and vigilance of divine providence. The text highlights that beings move in perfect correspondence with the spirit that animates them, teaching God's sovereign control over events.

outline.title: Glory departs and the temple is exposed
outline.explanation: The glory of the Lord leaves the entrance of the temple, lays upon the cherubim and goes to the east gate. Ezekiel acknowledges that the same beings seen in the river Chebar are there again, confirming the continuity of vision and concluding with the observation that each one moved in the direction of his face.

study.context: The notes link this chapter to Ezekiel's previous view of the Chebar River and the setting of the temple in Jerusalem. Tyndale observes that the temple was the terrenal place where the glory of the Lord could dwell among the people, but this permanence depended on the holiness of the people; in the face of contamination, glory departs. Matthew Henry also understands the chapter as preparation for the destruction of Jerusalem, with two main signs: the coals thrown over the city and the withdrawal of the glory of the temple. Adam Clarke says that the same majestic view reappears here, with signs that divine protection was about to be withdrawn.
study.theology: The chapter teaches that the presence of God is holy, personal and sovereign. The temple does not guarantee automatic protection when there is impurity and rebellion; glory can withdraw. The embers show that the judgment is real and will come upon the city. The wheels and cherubim, with eyes everywhere, communicate watchfulness and providential government: nothing escapes the Lord. The gradual withdrawal of glory also communicates the seriousness of divine separation, as if God confirmed, step by step, the breakage caused by sin. At the same time, the vision preserves the majesty of God: he is not defeated by Jerusalem, but acts freely in judgment.

scholarViews.insight: The eye-filled wheels show that the leaders' assertion that the Lord saw no situation was false; the vision responds directly to the spiritual blindness of the people.
When God comes out of a people, all judgments erupt upon him; the withdrawal of the glory from the temple prepares the ruin of Jerusalem.
The fire embers must mean that the city would be burned by the Chaldeans; the symbol announces the imminent fire.

questions: What does it mean, in practice, to treat the presence of God as holy, and not as an automatic guarantee of protection?
In what ways does the image of the wheels full of eyes correct our tendency to think that God does not see injustice?
Is there any area of our community or personal life in which the glory of God is being resisted rather than honorable?
study.practice: This chapter calls for reverence and repentance. The concrete application is to examine whether our life, worship and decisions are compatible with the holiness of God rather than presumed about his presence. It also calls us to trust that the Lord governs events accurately, even when his judgment seems severe. In practical terms, it is worth confessing specific sins, abandoning any empty religious trust and seeking a life of obedience that honors the glory of God in everyday life.
study.uncertainty: The text and notes provided do not definitively explain all the symbolic details of the wheels, faces and the structure of the view. Some descriptions are interpreted by the commentators as symbols of the divine government, but the exact meaning of each element remains, in the material provided itself, at the level of visionary image and not of closed definition.
